claims.text: The protective coating has a well-defined dual-phase FCC/BCC microstructure.
The initial microstructure was produced by rapid solidification followed by a tailored heat treatment.
The tailored heat treatment preserves sharp FCC/BCC phase boundaries.
Stable, sharp FCC/BCC interfaces govern the coating's superior creep resistance.
Sharp FCC/BCC interfaces inhibit dislocation climb.
Sharp FCC/BCC interfaces impede diffusion-driven creep deformation.
FCC/BCC phase boundaries act as dislocation-pinning sites and thereby retard creep under sustained loading.
A controlled mild heat treatment can blur the FCC/BCC interfaces.
At elevated temperature under sustained stress, plastic deformation in high-entropy alloys is typically accelerated by dislocation climb and diffusion.
Diffusing the FCC/BCC interfaces reduces the barrier to dislocation climb.
Reducing interface sharpness will increase creep strain.
The coating with preserved sharp interfaces will have a lower creep rate than the heat-treated coating with diffused interfaces.
The coating with preserved sharp interfaces will accumulate less creep strain over 100–300 hours than the coating with diffused interfaces.
At approximately 600°C and sustained sub-critical stress, creep is activated while the FCC/BCC structure remains below full homogenization or phase dissolution.
Interface sharpness should correlate positively with creep resistance.

contradictions.description: The starting material is repeatedly called 'as-deposited,' but it is also described as having already undergone a post-solidification tailored heat treatment. This makes it unclear whether the baseline is genuinely as-deposited or previously heat-treated.
